# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

## Respondents

Practitioners (primary link, `finance_lead`):
- Dana Whitfield: HN/47279411 ("we wouldn't want to switch even for a higher yield… the operational burden is more important to us than yield", "about 3.2%"). The $300k transfer is **[author]**.
- Marcus Oyelaran: HN/47279219 (self-directed brokerage, "more paperwork and back and forth", then "click that button now!"). The $3M and August are **[author]**.
- Lena Hofstra: HN/47279349 ("nowhere near juicy enough for me to literally bet the company on") and HN/47279304 (bank-run worry). The Treasuries-only policy and the two banks are **[author]**, after the 2023 bank failures the thread refers to.
- Tomás Reyes: HN/47283895 ("I’ve wanted this produce for years"), with the launch post's "large infusion from a raise". Cash sitting in plain checking is **[author]**.
- Aisha Karimi: HN/47279292 ("business savings accounts not much below this (2.85%) while keeping things safe (FDIC insured)").
- Ben Okafor: HN/47280707 (the fee "peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less"). The $1.5M is **[author]**.
- Rachel Lindqvist: HN/47282512 and HN/47283590 (PHC and QSBS: "a bunch of startups are raising $20m on $0 revenue … interest … can easily be the only income").
- Hiro Tanabe (gate No): HN/47279242 ("Startups otherwise are lean and won't hold enough cash to get a meaningful return").
- Grace Mbeki: HN/47283265 ("they might be better suited to deal with a fractional CFO service"). The Slack approval is **[author]**; the YC page (YCC) says the firm is reachable around the clock on Slack (paraphrased).
- Owen Castellano (chip): author's invention, filling a gap: no commenter refuses to say. A chipped story is needed so the reading counts one GUESSED person. It loosely echoes HN/47279377 (an investor steering portfolio companies).
- Nadia Seferović: HN/47286820 ("ask your bank manager for rates on a 30 day deposit account … it appeared in my online banking the next day").
- Kevin Duarte: the launch post ("a mutual fund where your principal is at considerable risk – it had a 9% loss in 2022") and HN/47280944 (the short-term bond fund in "one of the leading startup treasury products"). Moving the loss to August 2026 is **[author]**.

Decision-makers (`link: COMMERCIAL_B2B`, `founder`, Part 3 only, no story on screen):
- Sofia Marchetti: author's invention, filling a gap: the thread has almost no willing buyer. She stands for the founders' own case ("putting $5M into Palus yields them an extra $50k-75k per year", HN/47290584) and the batchmates who "wanted this too" (HN). Her $2,000 a month is the bank's treasury fee.
- Jamal Booker: HN/47297953 ("That 50-75k is more like $5k/month out of what is typically a ~200-400k monthly burn") and HN/47401784 ("it definitely takes weeks to diligence").
- Eleanor Vance: HN/47279349 ("bet the company"); the board having to agree is **[author]**.
- Ravi Menon: HN/47279377 ("I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries"). The investor who had to agree is his.
- Maya Feldman: HN/47283895 (signed up) and HN/47283356 (liked "a number that goes up").
- Daniel Osei: HN/47283590 ("The probability is Low but the impact for us is massive"). The tax adviser's long sign-off is his.
- Irene Kowal: HN/47279831 ("This should be a hard pass for literally everyone … SGOV") and HN/47279261 ("just put the money in a Bond ETF").
- Felix Brandt: HN/47282750 ("I am willing to take a little bit more risk for a higher return … an extra month or two of runway").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What would make it worth more?

whys.g1: The two groups are plain and right, but Felix Brandt's wish to see the actual yield after fees on paper belongs with 'The fee eats the extra yield' rather than sitting alone, and Daniel Osei's board worry could as well have gone with Ravi Menon's.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line, and Ravi Menon's board-approval story, the one answer not about price, was rightly left out of the groups.

founder.order_why: It runs from context to problem, idea, buyer and then sending, which is how I'd explain Palus myself; having the founder as buyer after the finance lead as user fits how a startup actually moves its cash.
founder.asked_twice: Screens 3 and 4 show the same kicker and the same question ('Before we test anything, let's define exactly where this idea applies'), so it reads as one question asked twice.
founder.missing: Nothing asks how much cash the company holds, and price can only be a money amount per period, not my 0.25% of the balance, so I had to guess a $4M–6M reserve to state $800–1,200 a month. There is also no way to say my real advantage is more yield (more money), only the five fixed codes. And the cost question doesn't make clear that the cost is yield given up rather than money spent.

COMMERCIAL_B2B.order_why: It runs from what idle cash cost me, to a fair fee and what would justify more, to who signs and how long diligence takes, to whether I'd move money, which is how I'd actually think it through, though the counter jumping from 2 of 6 to 4 of 6 looked like I'd skipped a screen.
COMMERCIAL_B2B.missing: Nothing on safety and access: where the money actually sits and whether it's insured or held in T-bills post-SVB, and how fast I can pull it back into operating when we need it.

screens.why5: The founder-decides, nobody-else belief is what I typed, but listing the board with no role next to it blurs that the board was only a possibility I raised, not someone who has to agree.
screens.instead: The people involved: finance lead · has the problem; startup founder · decides and pays; the board · may weigh in on the cash policy (not needed to buy)

screens.why1: Right after I named the board as the one who might have to agree, it makes sense to pick which belief to test: board sign-off or me deciding alone.
screens.why2: Mostly plain, but 'help managing the money they will not touch' is a clumsy stand-in for 'treasury' or 'idle cash', and 'Pick the one role' and the placeholder bar ('the one you pick had to agree') read oddly when the pick is 'Nobody else'.
screens.why3: Whether I would move the reserve on my own or take it to the board is exactly what I know as founder-CEO.
screens.why4: The board versus nobody else covers my two cases cleanly, with no overlap and nothing missing from what I listed.
screens.why5: The test Keel shows, 'the startup founder decides, and nobody else has to agree', is exactly my item.
screens.instead: Which do you want to test? Options: The board has to sign off / Nobody else, the founder decides alone. Bar: at least 2 in 3 founders say nobody else had to agree the last time they moved their treasury or idle cash.

screens.why1: After who has to agree, asking what slows the sale is the natural next step, and for me it is the real question: diligence is what kills a treasury switch.
screens.why2: Approvals, reviews, diligence, switching: every word is how I and the founders I sell to talk about moving a reserve.
screens.why3: I live these blockers every week, from founders asking for weeks of diligence to boards that need to bless where the cash sits.
screens.why4: It is a free box with one escape chip, 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a friction question I could choose to skip.
screens.why5: I typed three blockers, but Keel kept only diligence, dropped the board and the tax adviser, and invented 'about 4 weeks' when my material only says it 'takes weeks'.
screens.instead: What could slow or stop a startup moving its reserve to a new provider? Diligence on the provider; Board approval of the cash policy; A tax adviser's sign-off -- with the belief stating which one I expect to bite most, not a 4-week figure I never gave.

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow or stop a purchase, it's obvious Keel shows me its list back to check before it builds the belief on diligence.
screens.why2: Board approval of the cash policy, diligence on a new provider and a tax adviser's sign-off are exactly how a startup founder talks about moving the reserve, and the intro reads on first pass.
screens.why3: As the founder who signs where the reserve sits, I know exactly what has to clear before we move cash, since my own batchmates and the HN thread walked through these steps.
screens.why4: Keel's added 'A signed account agreement' is a formality every provider has rather than something that slows or stops a purchase, so it sits oddly next to the three real hurdles; the KYC and onboarding paperwork, the 'paperwork and back and forth' founders complain about, would have been the truer fourth line.
screens.why5: My three frictions are kept word for word, and the belief that most founders clear diligence within about 4 weeks, or skip it, matches the 'takes weeks to diligence' I took it from.
screens.instead: What has to happen first: Board approval of the cash policy / Diligence on a new provider / A tax adviser's sign-off / Onboarding and KYC paperwork

screens.why1: Right after I named what could slow a purchase, it asks which one step I want to time, so the reason it sits here is plain.
screens.why2: Board approval, diligence on a provider and a tax adviser's sign-off are the words I'd use myself, and 'how long would this step take before it went through' reads on first pass.
screens.why3: How long diligence on a treasury provider takes is something I know from my own batch, where the thread itself says it 'takes weeks', so my 4 weeks is an estimate from my own experience.
screens.why4: The three frictions I typed are there and distinct, and Keel's added 'signed account agreement' is a real and separate step in onboarding a custodian-held account, not a duplicate.
screens.why5: The test 'most startup founders would get through diligence on a new provider within about 4 weeks, or not need it' is my belief and my number, and the 'or not need it' fits my start-small, five-minute pitch.

screens.why1: After price, who must agree and what slows a purchase, it is the natural next question to ask what first commitment I want from the founder.
screens.why2: Plain to me, though "them" takes half a beat to resolve to the startup founder rather than the finance lead, and the belief line settles it.
screens.why3: The first step of onboarding is my own design, so I answer it straight from the launch thread: start small, try us out, grow your position.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape chip, and "Leave this out of the study" fits a free-text step I might not want tested.
screens.why5: "Move a small part of the reserve" is my answer word for word; "in most cases" and "now" frame it as a belief without changing what I meant.

screens.why1: After I typed my first step, it makes sense to check the short version strangers will hear and the bar it will be held to, as the last commercial item.
screens.why2: 'Move a small part of the reserve' is how I and other founders talk about long-term cash, so I can read it in one go.
screens.why3: Deciding whether to move some of our cash reserve is the founder's own call, so they can answer from what they would actually do.
screens.why4: The 'probably not or no' bar at 1 in 3 is fair, but the step never says where the money goes, so 'move it' leaves the destination (a new treasury provider) open.
screens.why5: My step was 'start small, try us out, and grow your position over time'; Keel kept 'small' but added 'now' and dropped the trial-then-grow sense, which makes it a slightly harder ask than mine.
screens.instead: Move a small part of the reserve to try it

screens.why1: Asking whether to offer a pilot right before the study goes out is the obvious last step, after I named the first real step I want from buyers.
screens.why2: 'Offer a pilot', 'Leave your email' and 'Pilot tab' are plain to a founder, and the hint shows exactly what respondents will see.
screens.why3: Whether I want sign-ups to try Palus is my own call, and I can answer it at once.
screens.why4: Yes or no covers it and the two options are distinct.
screens.why5: My commitment step, 'Move a small part of the reserve', is not in the line strangers get, so the pilot reads as a generic 'try this' rather than my start-small ask.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you move a small part of your reserve to try this for real? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Choosing who will put my questions to finance leads belongs right before the link goes out, after the study itself is settled.
screens.why2: The screen says I am picking a voice that Keel records once, but it also says the interviewer asks on video, so I have to read it twice to tell whether I am choosing a face, a voice or both.
screens.why3: I can play both 5-second samples and judge which one a US startup finance lead would take seriously, so this is my call to make.
screens.why4: Two named samples are enough to choose between, but nothing says how Daphne and Saskia differ (accent, tone, face), and an American-sounding voice matters to a US finance audience.
screens.why5: It still says finance leads, my respondents, and nothing about Palus or the founder role leaks into the choice.
screens.instead: Who should ask finance leads your questions on video? Daphne (US accent, calm and businesslike) ▶ 5 s · Saskia (British accent, warm) ▶ 5 s; the face and voice you pick are recorded once for this project, 400 credits either way.

screens.why1: Choosing how strangers will answer belongs right after choosing who asks them, just before sending.
screens.why2: The screen before said I was sending to finance leads, and now it says "founders", so I read it twice to work out whether it means the founders on my buyer questions or me.
screens.why3: I know my people: finance leads and founders at funded startups will happily tap through on a laptop, and I can judge whether they would talk to a video interviewer.
screens.why4: AI interviewer, read and tap, or let them choose covers the real choices without overlap, and the readiness notes say plainly what each one costs me in waiting.
screens.why5: My study is aimed at finance leads with founders only on the buyer part, so calling all respondents "founders" drifts from the roles I typed.
screens.instead: How should finance leads and founders answer? AI interviewer · Daphne / Read and tap / Let them choose

screens.why1: Once the questions and the interviewer are set, deciding who gets the link is the obvious last step before sending to batchmates' finance leads and founders. The 'SENT' kicker is a little premature, though.
screens.why2: Most of it is plain, but 'the Contacts page' names a part of Keel I haven't been shown, and each label runs straight into its description, so I read the second option twice.
screens.why3: I know exactly who I'd send this to: the batchmates who told us they wanted this, plus the finance leads and founders I can name.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and real, but I can't combine them, and I'd want named batchmates plus one open link posted in the YC founder channel.
screens.why5: Nothing here alters what I typed, and no product detail or role leaks into it.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? — People I know by name (a link each) / A list I search for in Keel (a link each) / One open link I post where they already are, e.g. a founder Slack (they sign in with Google) — and let me pick more than one.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits beside Existing sacrifice's 1 of 7, but two cards say the stronger 'Did not hold', so the headline is not the worst card the page says it uses.
screens.why_b2: Each card gives the count and the bar, but 'not holding' and 'did not hold' read as the same thing at first, and Existing sacrifice counts over 7 while the rest count over 8 with no reason given.
screens.why_b3: Buyer and payer, Purchase friction and Commitment carry the belief lines I checked word for word, and Price and Existing sacrifice use my 0.25% and 2% figures.
screens.why_b4: The cards say what went wrong, such as diligence most often taking 4 weeks to 3 months and only 4 of 8 moving now, but the page never says what to change, like aiming the pitch at board or diligence sign-off.
screens.why_b5: n=8 is visible, but nothing says 8 is a small sample, and 'smaller than you think' reads founders' fees and hours as if they were the yield given up I estimated.
screens.instead: Did not hold: diligence (5 of 8 over 4 weeks) and moving money now (4 of 8) block the sale, so plan for a weeks-long diligence pack and board sign-off, and note that 8 founders is a small sample.

screens.why_b1: Not holding up sits right beside 1 of 7 at or above 2% against a bar of 5 of 7, so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The strip shows 7 people and the marker at 5, but the 0 to 3 percent axis and the 5 of 7 count bar are two different bars on one chart, so it takes me a second look to see which is which.
screens.why_b3: My estimate was yield given up versus a bank treasury product, about $4k to $6k a month on a $5M reserve, but the card restates it as 2% of balance lost in the operating account, which I can still recognise but did not quite say.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the gap and points to the Price card, but it does not tell me whether to stop selling on the yield gap or to reframe the pitch against the treasury fee and rate.
screens.why_b5: n and the small group are said plainly, but 'smaller than you think: they lose less today' is a firm claim from 7 people, and the question about the operating account does not ask about the treasury yield gap I meant.
screens.instead: Among 7 founders only 1 puts missed interest at 2% or more, and most hold idle cash in a treasury product rather than the operating account, so ask what their current treasury earns and lead with the rate gap, not idle cash.

screens.why_b1: The verdict reads Not holding up, and right under it is 1 of 8 at 0.25% or more against a bar of 6 of 8, so I know the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b2: The bands show how many founders picked each fee, all 8 were counted, my 0.25% is marked as the low edge of its band, and the bar sits at 6 of 8, so I can read it on first look.
screens.why_b3: 0.25% a year on AUM is my fee, but I entered it in Keel as $800 to $1,200 a month, and 'of the balance per company a year' is clumsy wording, so I recognise it but it isn't quite the line I checked.
screens.why_b4: The So line names the most common pick (0.1% to under 0.25%), but then sends me to the Insights tab instead of saying what that means for my fee, for example a lower fee or one taken only on yield above the bank's rate.
screens.why_b5: The low n is stated ('a small group: a lean, not a call'), but Ravi's board-approval quote and Felix's paper-trial quote are both labelled 'One more thing · Price' when they are about approval and trust, not the fee, which suggests a price objection they never made.
screens.instead: Not holding up, a lean from 8: 7 of 8 founders put a fair fee below 0.25% and most chose 0.1% to under 0.25%, so try about 0.15%, close to what the bank's treasury already charges, or charge only on yield above the bank's rate.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits right beside '1 of 8 named your price or more · 5 needed', so I know at once that the check never got enough people to decide it.
screens.why_b2: The axis 0 to 2.5 has no unit, so I have to guess whether it is percent of the balance. The bar reads '1 of 1 (at least 2 in 3)', but the strip shows 1 cell for me and 4 ghost cells, so I have to stop and work out whether the base is 1 person or 5.
screens.why_b3: I recognise the 0.25% fee and 'paid out of the gain' as my own pitch, but Keel derived this belief and I did not type it. The question asks 'where would the money come from', yet the rule counts 'loses your price or more', which is a different thing from what was asked.
screens.why_b4: 'Ability to pay waits until 5 have' only says more answers are needed. It never draws the real point: 7 of 8 founders stopped below 0.25% or would not pay, so the price is my problem, not where the money comes from.
screens.why_b5: The screen keeps n visible and says 'a small group', but calling one person 'a lean' is a soft overstatement, and so is a chart that draws 1 of 1 as clearing an 'at least 2 in 3' bar.
screens.instead: Too few to call: only Maya would pay 0.25%, and she says it comes out of the gain. The other 7 named less or would not pay, so fix the price before this question matters.

screens.why_b1: The number is right beside the verdict (5 of 8 could sign alone, bar 6 of 8, 1 short), but "People disagree" doesn't tell me plainly whether my belief held, and the line under it opens on the minority instead of the call.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts sign-off answers over 8 founders, 5 for and 3 against, with the bar marked at 6. The strip makes it plain even though the "Yes" bar sits second, not first.
screens.why_b3: "Buyer and payer" and "The startup founder decides, and nobody else has to agree" are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: "Expect someone else's agreement in some deals" is true but generic, and it sends me to another tab for who that someone is, when that tells me what to prepare (a board pack, an investor note, a tax sign-off).
screens.why_b5: n=8 is visible, "a small group: a lean, not a call" says the n is low, and 1 short of the bar is not dressed up as either held or failed.
screens.instead: Just short: 5 of 8 founders could sign alone (bar 6); the other 3 needed a board, an investor or several people, so have a cash-policy page ready for the board in some deals.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside 5 of 8 expecting longer than 4 weeks against a bar of no more than 2 of 8, so I know the answer and the number that decides it at once.
screens.why_b2: The bands and counts are plain, but the bar is given two ways ("no more than 2 of 8" against in the verdict, "6 of 8" for on the chart and strip), and the stray "You said diligence on a new provider." line made me look twice.
screens.why_b3: The title Purchase friction and the belief line are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: It tells me to plan for a 4-week-to-3-month diligence cycle and points to the Insights tab for what eats the time, which is something I can act on in my sales plan.
screens.why_b5: My belief said "about 4 weeks", yet a 4-week answer falls in the against band whose low edge is my own number, so some of the five may be closer to my estimate than "did not hold" suggests, though the "a lean, not a call" caveat for n=8 is honest.
screens.instead: Did not hold: 5 of 8 founders expect diligence to take 4 weeks to 3 months, past your 'about 4 weeks' (bar: at most 2 of 8). With 8 people this is a lean, so plan a sales cycle of one to three months and see Insights for what slows it.

screens.why_b1: "Did not hold" sits right beside "4 of 8 said yes · bar 6 of 8 · 2 short", so I know the answer and the number that settles it in one glance.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts the yes / probably not / no answers (4, 2, 2) over the 8 founders who answered, and the strip puts the marker at 6 of 8, which matches "no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no" (at most 2 of 8 against).
screens.why_b3: The card is titled Commitment and its belief line is word for word the one I checked: "In most cases the startup founder would move a small part of the reserve now."
screens.why_b4: The So line only repeats the count and sends me to the Insights tab; it doesn't say what half the founders refusing even my "start small" step means for the pitch.
screens.why_b5: All 8 are shown and counted, and the screen says outright "a small group: a lean, not a call", so it claims nothing beyond these eight founders.
screens.instead: 4 of 8 won't move even a small part, and they include the ones who said a board, tax adviser or diligence must come first, so "start small" alone doesn't get past them; lead with what those gatekeepers need (see Insights).

screens.why_b1: Price, Purchase friction and Commitment each show a clear verdict beside the deciding number, but Buyer and payer says 'People disagree' over '5 of 8 · bar 6 of 8 · 1 short', which is a miss and should read as did not hold.
screens.why_b3: All four belief lines are the ones I checked on the way in, word for word, under the dimension names I know.
screens.why_b4: Nothing on the screen says what these whys mean for Palus, for example cutting the fee toward 0.1% or offering a paper trial before any money moves; it only lists quotes.
screens.why_b5: Buyer and payer lists Ravi, Eleanor and Daniel as 'never saw it', yet their answers about board calls and board comfort with mortgage bonds sit under Price, so three empty boxes read as if nobody gave a why when the why is one box up.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add things I did not type: founders compare the 0.25% fee to a one-point spread and want under 0.1%, boards balk at mortgage bonds specifically, a lead investor took two board calls, and one founder would watch it on paper for months before moving any cash.
screens.instead: Under Price: 'founders weigh the fee against the spread, not the balance; most named under 0.1%', with Ravi's and Daniel's board quotes shown under Buyer and payer and Felix's paper trial under Commitment, and one line on what to try next.

screens.why1: As the first screen on a buying-decision link, showing me the idea before asking whether I'd pay is the obvious place to start.
screens.why2: Plaid, checking and custodian are plain to me, but 'short-duration, floating-rate, government-backed mortgage bonds' is a bond desk's phrase I'd have to read twice, and I'd wonder whether 'mortgage' means risk.
screens.why3: Where our raise sits and what it earns until we spend it is exactly the call I make at Mercury every quarter.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options to judge.
screens.why5: It stays a treasury account for the reserve, in our name, back in one to two days, earning a 4.5 to 5 percent target, and nothing of the plan leaks beyond the idea shown on purpose.
screens.why6: Heard once, the four stacked qualifiers before 'mortgage bonds' are a mouthful I'd lose, though the rest says well.
screens.instead: Imagine Palus, a treasury account for reserves. It links to your bank through Plaid and holds your long-term reserve in government-backed bonds, in your company's name at a regulated custodian, with cash back in checking in one to two business days. The people building it believe it would earn the 4.5 to 5 percent it targets.

screens.why1: Right after the idea card about idle cash earning nothing, it makes sense to ask what leaving money in the operating account actually cost me.
screens.why2: Interest I missed is something I never saw, and I'd think of it in dollars a year, not as a percent of a balance that went up and down all year after the raise.
screens.why3: I know roughly what we held in Mercury and what treasury yields were, but the missed interest is a counterfactual I'd have to work out on the spot, so I'd be guessing.
screens.why4: A single percent box doesn't fit a balance that kept changing, and the 'None' chip overlaps with typing 0, which leaves two escapes where there should be one.
screens.why5: Nothing leaks, but the founder's case is dollars a year ($50k-75k on $5M), and asking for a percent of the balance drifts away from the way the cost is actually felt.
screens.why6: 'A percent of the balance last year, or a low and a high; none is 0' is a mouthful of instructions in one breath, and two ways out are offered.
screens.instead: Last year, about how many dollars of interest do you think you missed on cash sitting in your operating account? (a dollar box; escape: I can't recall)

screens.why1: Right after the screen asking how much interest I missed in the operating account, asking what fee I'd accept for a treasury account is the obvious next question for me as the one who pays for it.
screens.why2: A yearly percentage fee on the balance is how every treasury and sweep product I've looked at quotes itself, so I can answer on first read, though calling the fee 'small' nudges me before I answer.
screens.why3: I already pay a treasury fee through the bank and I compare yields against fees, so I'd answer from what I actually do, not a guess.
screens.why4: The bands run from under a tenth of a percent to one percent or more without overlapping, they cover where real treasury fees sit, and 'I wouldn't pay for this' plus 'I can't say' covers the rest.
screens.why5: It only says Palus charges a fee on the balance, which is the pricing I'd expect, and nothing of the founder's plan or internal terms comes through.
screens.why6: Four options followed by a two-band follow-up are easy to hold, but 'Or say you can't say' trips when heard and 'small fee' is extra weight in the stem.
screens.instead: Palus charges a yearly fee on the balance it holds. What fee would feel fair to you? Under 0.1% · 0.1% to under 0.25% · 0.25% to under 0.5% · 0.5% to under 1% · 1% or more · I wouldn't pay for this; spoken escape: 'Or say I can't say.'

screens.why1: Right after I named a fee range, asking what would make me pay more is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Fee on balance is plain to me, but 'you put Palus at' reads like I rated the product rather than picked a fee, so I'd read it twice.
screens.why3: I know what I'd need before paying more for treasury yield, like a better rate, same-day liquidity, or FDIC or T-bill safety, so I can answer from my own head.
screens.why4: It is a free-text box with no options.
screens.why5: It echoes my own fee answer and the Palus name I was already shown on the idea card, so nothing new leaks.
screens.why6: Spoken, '0.1% to under 0.25%' is a figure and symbol mouthful; it should be said in words, like 'a tenth of a percent to under a quarter of a percent'.
screens.instead: You said a fee of a tenth of a percent to under a quarter of a percent a year. What would make a higher fee worth it to you?

screens.why1: After asking what fee would feel fair, it makes sense to ask whether I could approve moving our raise cash into Palus myself or would need my co-founder or board to agree.
screens.why2: "Sign off" is exactly how I talk about approving where the company's cash sits, so I can answer it straight away.
screens.why3: I know who has to approve a treasury move at my company, whether that's just me or me plus the board, so I'm answering from what I do, not guessing.
screens.why4: The four cover the real answers, but "Yes" is buried second, and "someone else would have to agree" overlaps with "several people would have to agree" when the true answer for me is "my board would want a say"; the yes/no prefixes also don't fit an either-or question.
screens.why5: Palus is named on purpose after the idea card, and nothing of the founder's plan or role labels reaches me beyond that.
screens.why6: It's one question with four short options I can hold, but the yes/no tags on an either-or question make a few of them a mouthful, and "Or say you can't say" is an awkward thing to hear.
screens.instead: Could you sign off on Palus yourself, or would someone else have to agree? Options: I could sign off myself · My co-founder would have to agree · My board would have to agree · It would be someone else's decision; escape: I can't say

screens.why1: Once I've said I could sign off on Palus myself, it makes sense to ask how long checking out a new place to hold our cash would take before money moves.
screens.why2: Diligence on a new provider is a word I use all the time, from the raise and from picking Mercury, so I can answer straight away, though 'went through' is a touch vague about whether it means signed or funded.
screens.why3: I've never moved treasury cash to anyone but the bank, so I would be estimating how long my own checks and a word with my lead investor would take rather than recalling it.
screens.why4: The bands are distinct and cover everything from a quick check to never, 'It wouldn't be needed' fits a founder who would just sign up, and 'I can't tell' is the right way out.
screens.why5: It names Palus as already shown on the idea card and asks about my own diligence step, with nothing of the founder's plan or labels for me leaking through.
screens.why6: It is one short question, read as four options and then a two-way pick, which is easy to hold by ear, and the only clumsy phrase is '2 to under 4 weeks'.

screens.why1: After price, sign-off and diligence, asking whether I'd actually move money is the obvious last question.
screens.why2: I'd understand it, but I don't call our cash 'the reserve' — it's the money from the raise sitting at Mercury — and 'a small part' leaves me guessing whether that means $100k or $1M.
screens.why3: I'm the one who decides where our cash sits, so I can answer this straight from my own judgement.
screens.why4: There's one yes and two flavours of no; with no 'Probably yes', my honest answer, 'yes, after we've vetted them', has to round up to a firm yes or down to probably not.
screens.why5: 'Reserve' comes from the idea card's own wording rather than how a founder talks about raise cash, so the founder's phrasing has crept into the question a little.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, with three options I can hold after hearing them once, though the first option repeats the whole stem.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you move some of the cash from your raise into it, or not? — Yes, straight away · Yes, after vetting them · Probably not · No
